surface_summary: Walter Wentford, a reclusive rich man, is found brutally murdered near his cottage, with a mounted policeman also killed nearby. Suspicion falls on Kenneth McKay, a bank clerk in love with Wentford's niece, Margot Lynn, amid forged cheques and mysterious banknotes. The case appears to involve a complex web of deceit, forgery, and revenge.
accepted_facts: Walter Wentford was found murdered near his cottage.
Constable Verity was found shot dead nearby.
Two aces of playing cards were pinned to Wentford’s door after the murder.
Kenneth McKay cashed a forged cheque linked to Wentford’s account.
inferred_conclusions: Kenneth McKay forged the cheque and killed Wentford to cover his crime.
Margot Lynn was involved in Wentford’s murder due to secret relations.
The murders were random acts by unknown criminals without organized motive.
mechanism_description: Rufus Machfield and Antonio Lamontaine, former cardsharps, sought revenge on Wentford (alias Lynn) for a past swindle involving a rigged gambling scheme. They murdered Constable Verity to impersonate police and gain access to Wentford’s house, where they killed Wentford after deceiving him. They staged the scene with playing cards and planted forged cheques to mislead investigators and implicate Kenneth McKay. Their plan unraveled due to Reeder’s careful investigation and evidence gathering.
delivery_path: Lamontaine murders Constable Verity and hides his body.
Lamontaine dons police uniform and rides Verity’s horse to Wentford’s house.
Wentford opens door to disguised Lamontaine, who gains entry.
Machfield and Lamontaine kill Wentford inside the house.
They pin two aces to the door as a signal referencing their cardsharp past.
They remove Wentford’s body and place it by the roadside to be discovered.
They plant forged cheques and other false evidence to implicate Kenneth McKay.
outcome_result: Machfield and Lamontaine are caught and executed after Reeder exposes their elaborate scheme.

false_assumption.statement: Kenneth McKay forged the cheque and murdered Wentford to cover his crime.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: McKay was found with blood on his shirt cuff and was in debt, making him a plausible suspect. The forged cheque traced back to him reinforced the suspicion.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The true culprits were Machfield and Lamontaine, who orchestrated the crime to frame McKay and avenge past grievances.

supporting_points: Blood found on McKay’s shirt cuff.
He cashed a forged cheque linked to Wentford’s account.
He had financial troubles and a jealous relationship with Margot Lynn.
He was seen near Wentford’s house on the night of the murder.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: McKay’s presence and evidence were manipulated by the real culprits to mislead the investigation.

red_herrings.description: Margot Lynn’s secretive meetings and evasiveness suggested possible involvement.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was protecting family secrets and unaware of the murderers’ plans.

red_herrings.description: Kenneth McKay’s jealousy and financial troubles made him a prime suspect.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was manipulated and framed by the real culprits to divert suspicion.

closed_circle.rationale: The suspects were limited to those with access to Wentford’s house, motive related to financial and personal grievances, and opportunity during the time of the murders.

discriminating_test.design: Reeder arranges a controlled reenactment of the murder night, including the timing of the mounted policeman’s patrol and the arrival of the culprits in disguise. The test focuses on the feasibility of the murderers impersonating the policeman and gaining access to Wentford’s house, as well as the planting of evidence such as the playing cards and forged cheques.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The reenactment reveals that only Machfield and Lamontaine could have executed the murder and deception as planned, disproving McKay’s involvement.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The reenactment confirms the timing and method of the murderers’ approach and the impossibility of McKay’s presence during the crime.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all necessary clues including the missing aces from the card pack, the forged cheque traced to Machfield’s associate, and the timing of the mounted policeman’s murder. Reeder’s observations about blood transfer and the staged crime scene are clearly presented. The false suspicion on McKay is supported by circumstantial evidence but contradicted by logical inconsistencies and alibis. Careful attention to these details enables the reader to deduce the true culprits.
